analysis.one_liner: Bars lenders from issuing home mortgages to anyone without a Social Security number.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to committee and never received a vote; it died when the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal lending law to prohibit any mortgage on a person's primary residence if the borrower lacks a Social Security number. That would affect a small group—mainly noncitizens lawfully in the country who cannot get Social Security numbers. It never got a hearing or a vote and died at the end of the Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: The bill's intended beneficiaries would be people concerned about mortgage lending to borrowers who cannot be identified through a Social Security number; the bill itself frames the restriction as a fairness measure in lending. Borrowers without Social Security numbers would be the group directly affected by the prohibition.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a section to the Truth in Lending Act stating that no creditor may extend mortgage credit secured by a principal residence to any consumer who lacks a Social Security account number, overriding any state law to the contrary.
The stated aim, per the CRS summary, is to prohibit mortgages on principal residences for consumers without Social Security numbers.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers without Social Security numbers would lose access to home-purchase mortgages, including some lawfully present noncitizens. Mortgage lenders would lose a slice of potential customers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would bar home-purchase mortgages for anyone without a Social Security number, which would include many lawfully present noncitizens who cannot obtain SSNs, cutting off a path to homeownership regardless of their ability to repay.

It preempts state law and is written as an absolute prohibition, with no exception for other lawful proof of identity or for loans made to undocumented borrowers who use taxpayer identification numbers, which some lenders used to document repayment capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If enacted, the bill would have addressed a policy concern some raised after the housing crisis—credit extended without verifiable identity—but it targeted a narrow slice of lending and would have barred home purchase for people without SSNs even when they could afford a mortgage, while lenders would lose that customer base. Its actual effect was nil: it died without ever being considered.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee, and no vote ever happened; it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 14, 2011 and referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On March 23, 2011 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it stayed.
No further action was taken before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill never received a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lenders and borrowers who extend or seek mortgages without Social Security numbers are better off, since nothing changed. No one lost anything concrete; the bill simply never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; the bill simply never moved

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never advanced far enough for a party-split vote.

industries.note: Lenders would be barred from making mortgages to consumers without Social Security numbers, shrinking their pool of eligible borrowers. In practice the bill's death left current rules untouched.

industries.industry: Consumers without Social Security numbers seeking home loans
industries.note: People lawfully in the U.S. without SSNs, including some noncitizens, would lose access to home-purchase mortgages. The group is small but the effect on it is absolute.
